At the height of the trade war between Trump and China, tariffs were being announced almost weekly, and companies like Logitech quickly raised the prices of their products in the US significantly.

Earlier this year, the US Supreme Court ruled that these tariffs were illegal and must be refunded to manufacturers. However, no company has yet been seen passing the refunds on to customers, and a class action lawsuit is currently underway to try to correct this...

Trump Tariff Storm

Last year Trump seized on the issue of the US trade deficit with China, and seemed to fantasise that slapping hefty tariffs on Chinese-made products would force companies like Apple to move their production lines back to the US.

This was, of course, never going to happen. The US lacks the manufacturing infrastructure, expertise and cheap labour needed to make consumer electronics at the scale required by major brands.

Trump kept claiming that the tariffs would be paid by China, but the reality was that they were paid by the US brands importing the finished products, and these added costs were ultimately passed on to consumers in the form of higher prices. At the height of the storm, tariff rates briefly reached as high as 145%.

Take Logitech as an example. The company raised the prices of about half of its product range by up to 25%.

Consumers deserve refunds

The US Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to impose these tariffs unilaterally, and stated that companies must be refunded what they had paid. The refund process is currently underway.

The problem is that these costs were ultimately borne by consumers through higher prices, and no affected company has yet shown any sign of refunding customers.

The law firm CPM has filed a class action lawsuit against Logitech over this, demanding refunds for consumers who paid higher prices during the period the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac view

The principle behind the case is beyond dispute. Companies paid the tariffs, passed the extra cost on to customers, and are now getting refunds from the government. Morally, they should refund that portion of the purchase price to consumers who bought their products during that period.

However, putting this into practice is extremely challenging. Logitech would need to identify every single transaction made through its vast network of third-party retailers, track the prices consumers paid, and calculate what portion of that was attributable to tariffs.

If this lawsuit ultimately succeeds, it would set a very interesting precedent — though it has to be said that in class actions, the ones who really profit are usually the lawyers, while the compensation consumers actually receive tends to be very small.
